scenes.heading: Primary Key
scenes.subheading: The column that uniquely identifies each row
scenes.narration: A primary key is a column, or set of columns, whose value uniquely identifies every row in a table.

scenes.heading: Rules of a primary key
bullets: Each table has at most one primary key
It is the anchor other tables reference
scenes.narration: A primary key's values must be unique, so no two rows can share the same identifier. It can never be null, because every row needs an identity. A table has at most one primary key, which serves as its single source of identity. And it is the anchor that other tables reference through foreign keys.

scenes.heading: Defining a primary key in SQL
scenes.narration: Here the customer_id column is declared as the primary key. That declaration tells the database to enforce uniqueness and reject any null value for this column. As a result, every customer row is guaranteed a distinct, non-null identifier. This guarantee is what lets other tables reliably point back to a specific customer.

scenes.text: A primary key guarantees every row has a unique, non-null identity that the rest of the schema can rely on.
scenes.narration: The essential point is that a primary key gives every row a unique and non-null identity, forming the backbone of a well-designed schema.
